text: If you're my brother, come and fight me!
This one tap of yours costs the game company two hundred yuan.
Why pay that? The whole business is one sum:
what it pays for you must be less than what you top up.
But only about one player in ten ever pays.
So that one has to pay more.
A six-yuan first top-up gets your wallet open once;
the leaderboard keeps the big spenders paying more and more.
At one company, paying players top up over 400 yuan a month on average.
Free players are useful too: when big spenders cut people down, someone has to watch.
But two weeks later everyone's gone, and the big spenders have no one to cut.
So open a new server: back to level 1, race up the board again, pay all over again.
When the old servers empty out, merge them into one.
But new servers need new players, and new players cost money.
One company spends 60 to 80 percent of its revenue on promotion: buying the next you.
As long as it pays back, the loop keeps turning.
Players cost so much that ads can't be wasted on people who won't pay.
So it's tacky on purpose: whoever cringes swipes away, whoever stays will pay.
A celebrity? That costs a fraction of one percent of the budget.
So don't laugh at how tacky it is.
It isn't made for everyone. It's made for you, the one who pays.
